title: The full radio spectrum from ELF to gamma: who uses each band and why
summary: A layered atlas of radio bands and the wider electromagnetic spectrum.

blocks.heading: Gamma rays are not radio waves
blocks.body: The title spans the electromagnetic spectrum. Radio occupies its low-frequency end; infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays extend beyond it. Begin with the overview, then inspect the radio band you need. Boundaries are conventional and applications overlap them.

blocks.heading: Frequency rises; wavelength falls
blocks.alt: A logarithmic conceptual spectrum shows radio and microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays in order of increasing frequency. Wavelength decreases in that direction.
blocks.caption: Schematic boundaries, not an allocation chart or a wavelength-calibrated ruler. X-ray and gamma classifications also depend on origin and overlap in energy.

blocks.heading: One relationship lets you navigate
blocks.body: For a wave in vacuum, speed = frequency × wavelength. Using about 300 million metres per second, 1 MHz corresponds to roughly 300 m, 100 MHz to 3 m, and 10 GHz to 3 cm. Wavelength is a useful clue for antennas and structures; it is not by itself a complete propagation forecast.

blocks.heading: Below ordinary broadcast radio
rows: ELF · 3–30 Hz
Earth and ionosphere studies; extremely long wavelengths
Efficient radiating structures are enormous relative to human equipment
SLF · 30–300 Hz
Specialized low-frequency communication and geophysical work
Low bandwidth and demanding infrastructure
ULF · 300 Hz–3 kHz
Geophysical signals and specialized links
Do not confuse electromagnetic frequency with an audible sound wave
VLF · 3–30 kHz
Specialized maritime communication and navigation
Long wavelengths; specialized antennas and limited data rates
LF · 30–300 kHz
Navigation and time signals; broadcasting in some regions
Ground-wave and ionospheric effects depend on path and frequency
blocks.caption: A band name describes frequency, not blanket permission to transmit. Uses are examples; allocation and licensing are jurisdiction-specific.

blocks.heading: The bands most listeners encounter
rows: MF · 300 kHz–3 MHz
AM broadcasting, maritime services
Ground-wave coverage and changing nighttime sky-wave behavior
HF · 3–30 MHz
Shortwave, amateur and long-distance links
Ionospheric propagation can connect distant places and varies strongly
VHF · 30–300 MHz
FM broadcasting, aviation voice, amateur radio
Many terrestrial links depend heavily on antenna height and path
UHF · 300 MHz–3 GHz
Mobile systems, television, GNSS, some Wi-Fi
Compact antennas; obstructions and link design matter
blocks.caption: Examples occupy selected sub-bands. A device using “Wi-Fi” does not identify one universal frequency.

blocks.heading: Microwaves and millimetre waves
rows: SHF · 3–30 GHz
Radar, satellite links and several Wi-Fi bands
What antenna gain and path margin are available?
EHF · 30–300 GHz
Millimetre-wave links, radar and radio astronomy
How do obstruction and frequency-dependent atmospheric loss affect this path?
300 GHz–3 THz · submillimetre / terahertz region
Spectroscopy, imaging and research systems
What source, detector and atmospheric window can serve the task?
blocks.caption: Microwave is a broader customary term, not a separate exclusive row in the official VLF–EHF naming ladder.

blocks.heading: Beyond radio: change the source and detector
rows: Infrared
Thermal imaging, remote controls and optical communications
Heat sensing depends on emission and detector band; not all infrared means hot
Visible
Human vision, cameras, lighting and optical instruments
A narrow part of the spectrum is visible to people
Ultraviolet
Lithography, fluorescence and solar observation
Material interactions and exposure concerns differ from visible light
X-rays
Medical and industrial imaging, crystallography
High-energy photons can penetrate materials and are ionizing
Gamma rays
Nuclear processes, astronomy and controlled industrial uses
Often distinguished from X-rays by origin; energy ranges can overlap
blocks.caption: This is an orientation to applications, not instructions for radiation equipment.

blocks.heading: Higher frequency also means more energy per photon
blocks.body: Photon energy is proportional to frequency. Power is a different quantity: many lower-energy photons can deliver substantial power. Calling radio non-ionizing does not mean every radio-frequency exposure or transmitter is harmless. Frequency, field strength, exposure geometry and applicable limits all matter.

slides.title: I want a signal to travel beyond the horizon
slides.body: HF can use the ionosphere, but time of day, solar conditions, frequency and the path all affect the link. A higher transmitter power is not a substitute for a workable propagation path.

slides.title: I want a compact directional antenna
slides.body: A shorter wavelength can make a physically small aperture electrically large. Compare antenna dimensions in wavelengths, then account for efficiency, bandwidth and pointing requirements.

slides.title: I want to see a warm surface
slides.body: Start in an appropriate infrared detector band. Account for emissivity, reflections, distance and the instrument’s limits; apparent temperature is not automatically the object’s internal temperature.

slides.title: I want to identify a material
slides.body: Choose a measurement mechanism: radio-frequency resonance, infrared absorption, visible/UV spectroscopy or X-ray diffraction answer different questions. “More frequency” is not a universal upgrade.

blocks.heading: Read the scale
blocks.prompt: Approximately what is the free-space wavelength at 100 MHz?
blocks.explanation: 300,000,000 m/s divided by 100,000,000 cycles/s is 3 m.

blocks.heading: Separate wave types
blocks.prompt: A 1 kHz electromagnetic signal and a 1 kHz sound wave share what?
options: The same cycles per second, but different physical mechanisms
blocks.explanation: Frequency counts repetitions. Sound is a mechanical disturbance; electromagnetic waves are electric and magnetic fields. Their speeds and interactions are different.

blocks.heading: A spectrum chart is not a service licence
blocks.body: Band boundaries and national allocations answer different questions. To choose a transmitter frequency, consult the applicable current allocation, licence conditions and equipment rules. This atlas gives orientation; it does not establish an authorized channel.
